source_text: Ὅταν οὖν τὸ μὲν εἷναι ἓν τὸ θεῖον ὡς ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον κἂν μὴ θέλωσι τοῖς πᾶσι συμφωνῆται ἐπὶ τὰς ἀρχὰς τῶν ὅλων παραγινομένοις, ἡμεῖς δὲ κρατύνωμεν τὸν διακοσμήσαντα τὸ πᾶν τοῦτο τοῦτον εἶναι τὸν θεόν, τίς ἡ αἰτία τοῖς μὲν ἐπ᾿ ἀδείας ἐξεῖναι καὶ λέγειν καὶ γράφειν περὶ τοῦ θείου ἃ θέλουσιν, ἐφ᾿ ἡμῖν δὲ κεῖσθαι νόμον, οἵ ἔχομεν ὅ τι καὶ νοοῦμεν καὶ ὀρθῶς πεπιστεύκαμεν, ἕνα θεὸν εἶναι, ἀληθείας σημείοις καὶ λόγοις παραστῆσαι; Ποιηταὶ μὲν γὰρ καὶ φιλόσοφοι, ὡς καὶ τοῖς ἄλλοις, ἐπέβαλον στοχαστικῶς, κινηθέντες μὲν κατὰ συμπάθειαν τῆς παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πνοῆς ὑπὸ τῆς αὐτὸς αὐτοῦ ψυχῆς ἕκαστος ζητῆσαι, εἰ δυνατὸς εὑρεῖν καὶ νοῆσαι τὴν ἀλήθειαν· τοσοῦτον δὲ δυνηθέντες ὅσον περινοῆσαι οὐχ εὕρηνται, ὡς οὐ παρὰ θεοῦ περὶ θεοῦ ἀξιώσαντες μαθεῖν ἀλλὰ παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ ἕκαστος· διὸ καὶ ἄλλος ἄλλως ἐδογμάτισεν αὐτῶν καὶ περὶ θεοῦ καὶ περὶ ὕλης καὶ περὶ εἰδῶν καὶ περὶ κόσμου. Ἡμεῖς δὲ ὧν νοοῦμεν καὶ πεπιστεύκαμεν ἔχομεν προφήτας μάρτυρας, οἵ πνεύματι ἐνθέῳ ἐκπεφωνήκασι καὶ περὶ τοῦ θεοῦ καὶ περὶ τῶν τοῦ θεοῦ. Εἴποιτε δ᾿ ἂν καὶ ὑμεῖς, συνέσει καὶ τῇ περὶ τὸ ὄντως θεῖον εὐσεβείᾳ τοὺς ἄλλους προὔχοντες, ὡς ἔστιν ἄλογον παραλιπόντας πιστεύειν τῷ παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πνεύματι, ὡς ὄργανα κεκινηκότι τὰ τῶν προφητῶν στόματα, προσέχειν δόξαις ἀνθρωπίναις.
pass_a_gloss: When therefore the being one divine thing is agreed upon by almost all even if they do not want to, coming to the beginnings of all things, we however hold that the one who decorated all this is this God, what is the reason that for the ones it is permitted to speak and write about the divine things as they wish, but for us a law is laid down, we who have what we also think and have rightly believed, to show by signs of truth and words that one God exists? For poets and philosophers, as also for the others, have thoughtfully approached, having been moved by sympathy with the breath from God, by his own soul each one to seek if able to find and understand the truth; but having been able as much as to think around they have not found, as not having asked to learn about God from God but from himself each one; therefore each one of them has also been dogmatized differently about God and about matter and about forms and about the world. We however have prophets as witnesses of what we think and have believed, who by the inbreathed Spirit have proclaimed about God and about the things of God. You would say also, surpassing the others in understanding and in the piety concerning the truly divine things, that it is irrational having abandoned to believe in the Spirit from God, as having moved the mouths of the prophets like instruments, to pay attention to human opinions.

choices.english: as having moved the mouths of the prophets like instruments
rejected: as if instruments had been moved

pass_b_english: Nearly everyone agrees, even against their will, that a single divine principle underlies the origins of all things; we insist that the One who ordered the whole world is this God. Why, then, are others free to speak and write about the divine as they please, while we who both understand and rightly believe are bound by a law to demonstrate by signs of truth and reason that one God exists? Poets and philosophers, like everyone else, approached these matters thoughtfully. Moved by a kinship with the breath from God, each one's own soul stirred them to seek and, if possible, find and grasp the truth. Yet they only managed to speculate; they never found it, because they did not ask to learn about God from God but from themselves. Consequently, each one dogmatized differently about God, matter, forms, and the world. We, however, have prophets as witnesses to what we understand and believe. Inspired by the divine Spirit, they proclaimed the truth about God and the things of God. You yourselves would say the same: surpassing others in understanding and in reverence for the truly divine, you would call it irrational to abandon faith in the Spirit from God, who moved the prophets' mouths like instruments, and instead pay attention to human opinions.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Greek text. Pass A provides a literal rendering of the clauses, and Pass B provides a fluent English version that maintains the agency and theological distinctions of the original. Specifically, the distinction between learning 'from God' (παρὰ θεοῦ) versus 'from himself' (παρ᾿ αὐτοῦ) is preserved. The translation of 'ἐπὶ τὸ πλεῖστον' as 'by almost all' (Pass A) and 'nearly everyone' (Pass B) is an appropriate handling of the idiom. The relationship between the 'breath from God' (παρὰ τοῦ θεοῦ πνοῆς) and the 'soul' (ψυχῆς) is correctly rendered in both passes.

The translation accurately reflects the Greek text, preserving the meaning, structure, and key theological concepts. The citations and terminology are consistent with the source. The title 'Divine Truth and Testimony' appropriately captures the content of the passage.
